title: Household DNS filtering
body_md:
## DNS answers a name before a connection

When a device opens a site, it commonly asks a DNS resolver where that domain points. A filtering resolver may refuse names it classifies as malware or phishing. Cloudflare's **plain** 1.1.1.1 is a general resolver, not the same as its Families malware-filtering addresses 1.1.1.2/1.0.0.2. Families returns a blocking address for a classified domain. Other providers use different lists, categories, test pages and privacy policies. Select a provider only after reading its scope and data handling. DNS filtering can stop a known malicious domain before a page loads, but it cannot judge a seller's intent, inspect encrypted page content or reliably classify every new lookalike. A legitimate domain can be mistakenly blocked.

## Decide where the policy should apply

Configuring a router can cover devices that use its DNS settings while at home; configuring one device is narrower and easier to test. A local DNS blocker such as Pi-hole adds control but needs a maintained host and may expose query logs to its administrator. Browser secure DNS, a VPN, cellular data, a device's own DNS configuration or an app can use a different resolver. Thus “set on the router” does not mean “protects every device everywhere.” Encrypted DNS protects queries on the path to the chosen resolver; it does not automatically filter or validate websites. If another person manages the home network, agree on policy and a way to reverse it before changing shared settings.

## Test, investigate, reverse

Write down the original DNS setting before changing it. Use the resolver's documented safe test page or domain; do not test by visiting a live malicious site. Check a device on home Wi-Fi and, separately, cellular or another network if relevant. If a needed site fails, check whether the filter blocked its domain rather than assuming the site is dangerous. Confirm the service's true address independently, inspect the provider's block reason and consider a narrow exception only if you trust the destination. Avoid a broad allowlist of ad/tracking domains to fix one login. If the resolver is unavailable, restore your recorded settings or use a trusted fallback. DNS is a layer beneath browser warnings, updates, MFA and independent verification; a successful DNS lookup is never a safety verdict.

widget_config.goal: Set one household DNS filter deliberately, test its scope, and recover from a false block without abandoning safer browsing habits.
widget_config.today_action: Identify your current DNS provider on one device, choose whether filtering is wanted, then test a documented provider test domain on that device and note whether mobile data or browser secure DNS bypasses the setting.
widget_config.scope: General home-network explanation checked 2026-10-20. Cloudflare addresses are examples of one provider, not a universal recommendation; test names and router behavior vary. DNS labels can be wrong or late.

blocks.title: A new fake benefits from the gap
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a family member receives a parcel notice pointing to parcel-status.example. The filter allows it because the fictional domain is not classified.
blocks.analysis: An allowed DNS answer is only a name lookup. They open the real retailer order history through a saved app and do not enter credentials at the message address. The .example address is synthetic and not meant to be visited.

blocks.title: School portal blocked by category
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a known school portal stops loading after the household enables an aggressive category list; the school confirms its official domain independently.
blocks.analysis: This can be a false positive. The family inspects the resolver log or test result, reports the classification and, if necessary, adds only that verified domain as an exception. Disabling all filtering is not the only option.

blocks.title: Pilot a home DNS policy
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise: you are setting a test device before changing the shared router; no live risky domain is opened.

steps.prompt: You want malware filtering and see 1.1.1.1 and 1.1.1.2. Which choice?

choices.text: Use the documented Families malware-filtering address on the test device.
choices.consequence: The chosen resolver has the requested category.
choices.explanation: Plain 1.1.1.1 is not the Families filter.

choices.text: Use plain 1.1.1.1 and assume it blocks malware.
choices.explanation: Resolver names and policies must be checked, not guessed.

steps.prompt: How will you verify filtering without browsing a real scam?

choices.text: Search for a current malware link and open it.
choices.explanation: Never require a live malicious destination for a lesson or setup test.

choices.text: Use the provider’s documented safe test domain and record the result.
choices.consequence: You test the setup without exposure to a malicious page.
choices.explanation: Provider test endpoints are built for this purpose.

steps.prompt: The test works on Wi-Fi but not on cellular. What does that mean?

choices.text: The device may use different DNS on cellular; document the boundary.
choices.consequence: You know where the policy applies.
choices.explanation: Router DNS does not follow the phone off the home network.

choices.consequence: You may change a working setup for the wrong reason.
choices.explanation: Different networks commonly use different resolvers.

steps.prompt: A verified school portal is blocked after a category update.

choices.text: Turn off all protection and never revisit it.
choices.consequence: Every category is abandoned for one exception.

choices.text: Check the block reason and permit only the verified domain if needed.
choices.consequence: School access returns while most filtering remains.
choices.explanation: False positives call for a narrow, reversible response.

blocks.debrief: Replay by distinguishing the resolver selected, the network path actually used and the separate decision whether a site is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: What does plain Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 do in this lesson?

choices.text: Resolves names without the Families malware category.
choices.explanation: The filtering service has distinct addresses.

choices.text: Guarantees that every phishing domain is blocked.
choices.explanation: Neither plain DNS nor a filter can guarantee that.

questions.prompt: A filtered domain resolves successfully. What can you infer?

choices.explanation: DNS does not authenticate a seller.

choices.text: Only that this resolver did not block this lookup.
choices.explanation: A new or misclassified scam site can pass.

questions.prompt: Why may a browser ignore your router’s DNS filter?

choices.text: Its secure-DNS setting may use another resolver.
choices.explanation: Some browser configurations choose their own path.

choices.text: Router DNS always controls all browser queries.
choices.explanation: That ignores secure DNS and other overrides.

questions.prompt: A known service is blocked. Best first step?

choices.text: Assume it is criminal and warn everyone.
Independently confirm its domain and inspect the block reason.
choices.explanation: It could be a true or false positive.
